findings.title: Arbitrary HashMap growth from network data causes DoS via memory exhaustion
findings.impact: Table parsing (lines 139-155) creates a HashMap with no limit on key count. A single malicious frame can declare a table of 1000000+ entries, exhausting heap memory regardless of frame size declaration.
findings.evidence: Line 145: 'new HashMap<String, Object>()' with no capacity check. Line 151-152: silently ignores duplicate keys but adds all unique ones. No cardinality limit on table contents.

findings.title: Missing array size validation allows large array allocations
findings.impact: Line 68 in readShortstr() allocates a byte array of size read from unsigned byte (0-255) without validation. While this specific case is bounded by 255 bytes, similar pattern in readBytes() (line 88) allocates up to Integer.MAX_VALUE. An attacker can declare a 2GB array to exhaust memory.
findings.evidence: Line 68: 'new byte[in.readUnsignedByte()]' - bounded by 255, acceptable. Line 88: 'new byte[(int)contentLength]' - can be up to 2^31-1 bytes (2GB). No sanity check on declared size vs. actual stream size.

findings.title: Hard-coded UTF-8 string instead of StandardCharsets constant
findings.impact: Line 70 uses 'new String(b, "utf-8")' with hard-coded string. This re-parses the charset name on every call, incurring CPU overhead. If the string is misspelled, an UnsupportedEncodingException is thrown at runtime instead of compile-time.
findings.evidence: Line 70: 'return new String(b, "utf-8");' Hard-coded string literal.

findings.title: Long multiplication overflow in timestamp conversion silently produces wrong dates
findings.impact: Line 269 multiplies readLong() by 1000 without overflow check. If the timestamp value > Long.MAX_VALUE/1000, multiplication silently wraps to a negative or incorrect value, producing a wrong Date object. Applications relying on timestamp correctness could accept stale/future-dated messages.
findings.evidence: Line 269: 'return new Date(in.readLong()*1000);'. No Math.multiplyExact() or bounds checking. Long.MAX_VALUE = 9223372036854775807; dividing by 1000 gives max safe input of 9223372036854775L.

findings.title: Unbounded BigInteger/BigDecimal construction from network data
findings.impact: Line 175 constructs BigInteger and BigDecimal directly from 4-byte unsigned input without magnitude limits. While 4 bytes limits the exponent, the scale field at line 172 is also unchecked. A scale > Integer.MAX_VALUE or < Integer.MIN_VALUE passed to BigDecimal constructor could cause issues. No validation of numeric range.
findings.evidence: Line 172: 'int scale = in.readUnsignedByte();' - reads into int but should be 0-127. Line 175: 'new BigDecimal(new BigInteger(unscaled), scale)' with no bounds check on scale.

findings.title: Available() loop condition unreliable for stream position determination
findings.impact: Lines 244 and 148 use 'while(.*In.available() > 0)' to detect end of stream. The available() method is not guaranteed to return exact byte counts and may return 0 even when data remains (e.g., after blocking reads or with certain stream implementations). This can cause premature loop exit, leaving data unread and corrupting subsequent frame parsing.
findings.evidence: Line 148: 'while(tableIn.available() > 0)' in readTable(). Line 244: 'while(arrayIn.available() > 0)' in readArray(). Both rely on TruncatedInputStream.available() being accurate after partial reads.

findings.title: No timeout protection on stream I/O operations
findings.impact: readFully() calls (lines 69, 89, 174) will block indefinitely if the stream stalls or the peer never sends the declared number of bytes. A slow or malicious peer can cause thread deadlock. This is a thread-level DoS if connections are not bound to a timeout.
findings.evidence: Lines 69, 89, 174: 'in.readFully(...)' with no timeout. If stream is exhausted before expected bytes arrive, the thread hangs forever.

findings.title: Unvalidated recursive table/array nesting allows stack exhaustion
findings.impact: Malicious AMQP frames with deeply nested tables (line 181: case 'F') and arrays (line 184: case 'A') can cause StackOverflowError. readFieldValue() calls readTable() which calls readFieldValue() recursively with no depth limit.
findings.evidence: Lines 139-155 (readTable), 158-221 (readFieldValue), 237-249 (readArray). No MAX_NESTING_DEPTH or depth counter. Recursive calls at lines 181 and 184 are unbounded.

findings.title: Duplicate table keys silently discarded without error reporting
findings.impact: Lines 151-152 check 'if(!table.containsKey(name))' and skip duplicate keys silently. Malformed or attack frames with duplicate keys will not raise an exception; the first value is retained and later values are discarded without trace. This can hide frame corruption or attacks.
findings.evidence: Line 151-152: conditional put() with no error case. No log, no exception, no counter when duplicates are skipped.

findings.title: No validation of unsigned int bit shift positions in readUnsignedInt()
findings.impact: Line 233 performs bit shifts ('ch1 << 24', 'ch2 << 16', etc.) on long values read from individual bytes. While the logic is correct, it reinvents the wheel compared to DataInputStream.readInt(). The manual byte-by-byte reading is more error-prone and harder to audit than platform-provided methods.
findings.evidence: Lines 224-233: Manual unsigned int parsing via four read() calls and bit shifts. This is functionally equivalent to readInt() but obfuscates intent and audit surface.

defects_to_look_for.mechanism: A length field read from untrusted input decides the size of a buffer, and that buffer is created before the corresponding payload has been shown to exist.
Decoding routines call one another in a cycle with nothing counting how deep the cycle has gone, so nesting in the input controls the depth.
